problem: Prior object-search methods cover either space (scene graphs, object maps) or time (video/temporal reasoning), and dynamic scene graphs that do both assume closed vocabularies and fixed relations. No prior work retrieves arbitrary open-world objects described with attribute, spatial and temporal references while acting in the environment.
motivation: Service robots get requests like 'the mug that was here yesterday', where memory can be stale and the target may sit in a closed receptacle. The robot must decide when to trust recalled memory (search in time) and when to act and look (search in space). Existing benchmarks assume static scenes or passive video QA, so none test this.
key_idea: Put memory queries over a non-parametric long-term memory and embodied skills (navigate, detect, pick, open) into one unified tool action space, so an LLM policy interleaves search in time and search in space in a single decision loop with a working memory.
insight: Temporal retrieval alone (TR+S) and scene graphs (SG+S) have complementary strengths, and combining recall with active physical verification beats both. STAR has a larger share of physical actions than TR+S, which lets it fix stale memory. On interactive search it clearly beats TR+S, e.g. Spatial-Temporal Oracle 0.61 vs 0.17. Because STAR keeps raw images in memory and can revisit them, it also disambiguates similar receptacles where scene graphs fail.
method: Non-parametric long-term memory: vector database of records m_t=(timestamp, pose, caption embedding, raw image), with semantic, temporal and spatial indices built task-agnostically from patrol observations.
Working memory H: task-relevant action-outcome trajectory H_k=(a_1:k-1, y_1:k-1), initialized at task time and appended after each action, so the policy does not need the whole memory in context.

Unified action space: tools F with arguments θ, covering temporal actions (semantic/temporal/spatial memory queries returning top-r records) and spatial actions (navigate, detect, pick, open) that return perception or success feedback.

LLM policy with budget awareness: GPT-o3 picks one tool call per step from π(a|ℓ,H_k,R_k), with the remaining step budget R_k in its context; the loop stops on retrieval or when the budget is exhausted.

STARBench: VirtualHome benchmark of 360 tasks (225 visible, 90 interactive, 45 commonsense) over 3 scenes, with 3-6 days of patrol history and five instruction families (class, attribute, spatial, spatial-temporal, spatial-frequentist).

setting.backbone: GPT-o3 (frozen LLM policy) with a captioner/embedding model for memory
setting.observation: egocentric RGB observations with pose and timestamps, plus captions; simulator segmentation masks used for detection
setting.action_space: tool calls: memory queries (semantic/temporal/spatial) plus navigate, detect, pick and open skills; K=20 step budget
setting.simulator: VirtualHome (Unity3D) plus a real Tiago robot in a mock apartment
setting.privileged: Oracle mode uses GT object class labels in captions; all modes use simulator segmentation masks for detection; baseline SG+S uses GT scene graphs with GT data association

numbers.extra: Oracle memory (GT class labels); K=20; 18 tasks per family

numbers.eval_set_note: 9 tasks per type, 54 in total, Tiago robot in mock apartment

numbers_note: Main Visible Object Search results (45 tasks per type) are only in a bar-chart figure, so no exact values are available. Interactive results only in Table 2, with Oracle and Realistic columns; only a few rows are listed here. Table 2 also has A 0.50/0.61, S 0.50/0.50, ST 0.61/0.28, SF 0.61/0.44 (Oracle/Realistic). Real-world Table 5 also has Attribute 0.78, Spatial-Temporal 0.56, Spatial-Frequentist 0.56, Common-Sense 0.33. Success rates are converted from fractions to percent.
results: STAR beats the Random, SG+S and TR+S baselines on the visible, interactive and commonsense tasks. For example, commonsense success is 0.57 vs 0.19 for TR+S (Oracle). On interactive tasks Oracle success is 0.50-0.67 vs 0.17-0.56 for TR+S. On the real Tiago it is at least as good as TR+S on every type (e.g. class-based 0.67 vs 0.44). It uses about 1.5-2x the minimal number of physical actions.
limitations: Physical actions are inefficient (about 1.5-2x optimal); no explicit optimization of physical action cost.

Small evaluation: 3 VirtualHome scenes, few object classes, 9 tasks per type on the real robot, with wide confidence intervals; STAR is not better than TR+S on some real-world types (Spatial-Temporal, Common-Sense have no gain). STAR in Realistic mode drops on spatial-temporal interactive tasks.
Relies on simulator segmentation masks for detection and an expensive proprietary LLM (GPT-o3); memory has no forgetting or pruning.
